result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.greedy_color()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Color the graph using a greedy algorithm. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L57202-L57370){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.greedy_color( strategy="largest_first", interchange=False, seed=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Greedy coloring](/assets/graphs/greedy-color.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A strip of four triangles on six nodes, each node filled with the color of its class: C and F in the accent color, A and D in teal, B and E in violet. No edge joins two nodes of the same color, and the card lists the three classes 0, 1, 2." width="100%"} Graph coloring assigns colors (represented as integers) to nodes such that no two adjacent nodes share the same color. The greedy algorithm processes nodes in a specified order and assigns the smallest available color to each node. The result is always a valid coloring, but not necessarily one with the fewest possible colors; the node ordering chosen by `strategy=` largely determines how many colors end up being used. Coloring is a way of splitting nodes into conflict-free groups. Typical uses include: - scheduling (exams, meetings, or jobs that conflict get different time slots) - register allocation and frequency assignment (interfering items get different slots) - partitioning work into batches where no two items in a batch interact - getting a quick upper bound on the chromatic number (see `chromatic_number_upper_bound()`) Edge direction is ignored: in a directed graph, `A -> B` still forbids `A` and `B` from sharing a color. Self-loops are ignored. Every node in the graph receives a color, and isolated nodes always get color `0`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [strategy]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["largest_first"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : The strategy for ordering nodes during coloring. Options are: `"largest_first"` (the default), `"smallest_last"`, `"saturation_largest_first"` (alias `"dsatur"`), `"independent_set"`, `"random"` (alias `"random_sequential"`, as in NetworkX), and `"arbitrary"`. Matching is case-insensitive. See the *Strategy Types* section for how each one works. An unrecognized name raises a `ValueError`. [interchange]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to apply the color-interchange optimization. When a node would otherwise need a brand-new color, the algorithm first tries to free an existing color by swapping two colors along a *Kempe chain* (a connected run of nodes using just those two colors), which keeps the coloring valid. This usually saves colors at a modest extra cost, though as a heuristic it can occasionally use one more. It works with the `"largest_first"`, `"smallest_last"`, `"random"`, and `"arbitrary"` orderings; DSATUR and `"independent_set"` choose their own order and raise a `ValueError` when combined with it. Default is `False`. [seed]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Random seed for the `"random"` strategy. The same seed always gives the same coloring of the same graph; if `None` (the default), the order is drawn from system entropy, so repeated calls can differ. Ignored by the other strategies. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict[int, int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A dictionary mapping every node ID to its assigned color (0-indexed integers). The colors are consecutive integers starting from 0. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `strategy=` is not one of the recognized names, or if `interchange=True` is combined with `"saturation_largest_first"`/`"dsatur"` or `"independent_set"`. ::: ## Strategy Types {.doc-strategy-types} There are several strategies that can be used: - `"largest_first"`: process nodes in order of decreasing degree; handles the most constrained nodes early and is fast - `"smallest_last"`: repeatedly remove a minimum-degree node, then color in the reverse of that removal order; often produces optimal or near-optimal colorings on sparse graphs - `"saturation_largest_first"` or `"dsatur"`: DSATUR algorithm that always colors next the node with the most differently-colored neighbors (ties broken by degree); often produces the fewest colors - `"independent_set"`: repeatedly extract a maximal independent set from the uncolored nodes (favoring high-degree nodes) and give the whole set one color - `"random"` or `"random_sequential"`: shuffled node ordering; pass `seed=` for a reproducible result, or leave it unset to get a different ordering on each call - `"arbitrary"`: process nodes in the graph's internal storage order ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Greedy coloring is what every graph-coloring course starts with and what most real software uses in practice, despite its worst-case wastefulness. For any ordering it uses at most $\Delta(G) + 1$ colors, where $\Delta$ is the maximum degree, since a node can never have more than $\Delta$ already-colored neighbors. Even a bipartite graph (which needs only $2$ colors) can receive many more under an unlucky ordering. The `strategy=` argument controls this crucial ordering step. *DSATUR* (Brélaz, 1979) is the strongest general-purpose choice: it colors the highest-saturation node next, meaning the node whose neighborhood already uses the most distinct colors, and consistently produces optimal or near-optimal colorings for typical graphs. *smallest_last* peels the minimum-degree node last and applies its coloring in reverse peeling order, matching DSATUR on many sparse inputs; *largest_first* is faster but coarser. Because the underlying problem is $\mathsf{NP}$-hard, none of these strategies guarantees the true chromatic number, but running several and taking the best is a cheap and effective heuristic. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A 4-cycle is bipartite, so a greedy coloring only needs 2 colors, alternating around the square. Mapping IDs to labels makes the alternation easy to see: ::: {#9d4c5d23 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A")]) ) coloring = graph.greedy_color() # A and C share one color, B and D the other {graph.get_label_from_id(nid): color for nid, color in sorted(coloring.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'A': 0, 'B': 1, 'C': 0, 'D': 1} ``` ::: ::: A triangle is a different story: since every node is adjacent to both others, no two can share a color, so 3 colors are required no matter which strategy is used: ::: {#a2c4a83c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) ) coloring = graph.greedy_color(strategy="dsatur") num_colors = len(set(coloring.values())) # Returns 3 (colors for a triangle) num_colors ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 3 ``` ::: ::: On larger graphs the strategy matters. Counting the colors each strategy uses on the same random graph shows that DSATUR and the independent-set approach need one color fewer here than the simple orderings: ::: {#112efca2 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_gnm_graph(n=30, m=80, seed=23) strategies = ["largest_first", "smallest_last", "dsatur", "independent_set", "arbitrary"] {s: len(set(graph.greedy_color(strategy=s).values())) for s in strategies} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'largest_first': 5, 'smallest_last': 5, 'dsatur': 4, 'independent_set': 4, 'arbitrary': 5} ``` ::: ::: Color interchange can rescue a weaker ordering. On the same graph, `"largest_first"` needs one color fewer once it may swap colors along Kempe chains instead of opening a new color: ::: {#3fd218a9 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( len(set(graph.greedy_color().values())), len(set(graph.greedy_color(interchange=True).values())), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (5, 4) ``` ::: ::: The `"random"` strategy draws a fresh ordering on every call unless `seed=` is given. Running it with several seeds and keeping the best result is a cheap way to search for a coloring with fewer colors: ::: {#9485aca1 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} min(len(set(graph.greedy_color(strategy="random", seed=s).values())) for s in range(20)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 4 ``` ::: :::
